item.title: PEI’s fall fiscal update highlights economic resilience and improved net debt outlook
item.description:
PEI’s fall fiscal update highlights economic resilience and improved net debt outlook jenniferdhogan Fri, 10/30/2026 - 15:57

The Minister of Finance Jill Burridge released the Island’s fall fiscal and economic update for fiscal year 2026-27. 

Second quarter (Q2) results provide a mid-point update on provincial spending and the Island’s economic conditions, reflecting government’s efforts to deliver essential public services, managing expenditures and debt, and support economic growth.

“Island workers and businesses are working hard, and we continue to see that reflected in the resilience of our economy despite global uncertainty. Just as Island households make thoughtful financial decisions every day, government is doing the same. Our focus remains on maintaining essential programs and services, like healthcare and public education, while balancing responsible spending, careful debt management, and strategic investments that will support sustainable, long-term economic growth.”

- Minister of Finance and Affordability Jill Burridge

The updated forecast for fiscal year 2026-2027 is a deficit of $459.3 million, a $49.4 million increase from the 2026-2027 budget estimates presented in April 2026. The increased operating expenses of $101.3 million can be primarily attributed to the delivery of health care services, social program funding, and the rising fuel costs

Government revenues outperformed Spring 2026 budget estimates by $52 million thanks to stronger corporate income tax and sales tax revenues, and additional federal funding. Despite the rising financial pressures to maintain public programs and services, Prince Edward Island’s net debt position is improving by an estimated $101.8 million. The net debt-to-GDP ratio budgeted at 38.1 per cent has been reduced to 36.4 per cent, below the 40 per cent guardrail.

While expenditures have increased, the Q2 update shows PEI’s strong and resilient economy is contributing to improved revenues. Key indicators for the Island economy show year-to-date changes in 2026 compared to the same periods in 2025.

Population (July to July): 

  • Prince Edward Island’s population increased by 0.8% to reach 182,989 residents.

Labour participation (January to September):

  • Employment: The average monthly employment increased 3.1% compared to the same period last year.
  • Unemployment rate: PEI’s unemployment rate fell to 7.4%, representing a 0.7% decrease from the previous year.

Income (January to June): 

  • Labour income grew by 7.1%, exceeding the province’s Spring 2026 forecast of 4%. 
  • Working Island residents earned an average of $1,181 weekly.

Construction (January to September):

  • Housing starts: Residential construction continues to demonstrate strong activity with 1,442 starts. 
  • Value of non-residential construction is down 15.3%.

PEI economic sectors (January to August):

  • Exports: PEI’s international goods exports increased by 7.2%.
  • Tourism: Air, ferry, and road travel to Prince Edward Island, as well as overnight stays, are on pace for another record tourism year.
  • Farm cash receipts were up 3.5%.

Learn more about Prince Edward Island’s second quarter economic and fiscal updates here.

 

Media contact:
Vicki Tse
Department of Finance and Affordability
vickitse@gov.pe.ca

 

Backgrounder:

Economic update:

Economic data is reported on a year-to-date basis using various surveys and compares results to the same period from the previous year.

  • PEI's population was estimated at 182,989 on July 1, 2026, an increase of 0.8% compared to a year earlier
  • Average monthly employment for the first nine months of 2026 was up 3.1 per cent compared to the same period in 2025.
  • The average monthly unemployment rate fell by 0.7 percentage points to 7.4%.
  • Labour income grew 7.1% year-to-date through June, trending above the budget forecast of 4.0% for 2026. Average weekly earnings of $1,181 year-to-date through July were up 5.1%, in excess of inflation.
  • Retail sales grew 7.4% or $163 million year-to-date through July, on track to exceed the budget forecast of 3.0%.
  • Housing construction activity remains nearly on par with 2025’s high level of activity, with 1,442 starts through the first three quarters.
  • International goods exports were up 7.2% year-to-date through August, largely reflecting growth in the repair category of special transactions trade.
  • Tourism statistics show bridge, air and ferry traffic on track for record years through September and overnight stays are also on pace for a record year.

Fiscal update:

The baseline assumptions and projections are based on Spring 2026 information to develop the 2026-27 budget estimates. As the year progresses, based on operational needs, influences of global events, and other factors, the province’s fiscal and economic position will change.

Spring 2026 estimates include:

  • Total revenues: $3,386.3 million
  • Total expenditures: $3,796.2 million
  • Deficit: $409.9 million
  • Total net debt: $4,504.8 million
  • Total net debt-to-GDP: 38.1%

Q2 fiscal and economic update include:

  • Total revenues: $3,438.2 million
  • Total expenditures: $3,897.5 million
  • Deficit: $459.3 million
  • Total net debt: $4,403.0 million
  • Total net debt-to-GDP: 36.4%

Supplementary Departmental Summary

  • Health PEI is forecasting an increase in expenditures of $74.3 million from their Operating Budget. Key pressures include agency staffing, wage levies and salary premiums, out-of-province contracted services, medical supplies, and equipment and software pressures. These pressures are partially offset by salary vacancies/savings and delayed implementation of initiatives.
  • Innovation PEI expenditures are forecasted to be $23.3 million over budget, primarily due to significantly higher-than-anticipated performance related to the Aerospace and Defence Tax Rebate program. This is partially offset by an increase in expected Corporate Income Tax revenue from this sector.
  • The Department of Energy expenditures are anticipated to be $12.6 million over budget, largely reflecting increased Oil to Heat Pump Affordability (OHPA) grants to clear approved client backlogs before federal funding deadlines. This overage is fully offset by additional revenue of $12.9 million.
  • The Department of Health and Wellness is forecasting an expenditure increase of $12.1 million, due to prescription drug programs, Aging with Dignity initiatives carried forward from the prior year, Digital Health operating costs, At Home Caregiver Benefit program client growth, Chief Public Health Office vaccine and drug costs, and remaining Alliance for Mental Wellbeing wind-up commitments. These overages are fully offset by additional revenue.
  • The Department of Social Development and Seniors is anticipating an increase in expenditures of $4.3 million compared to Budget. This is primarily driven by a $5.8 million increase in AccessAbility Supports due to caseload growth, $800 thousand for the Seniors Hearing Aid Rebate Program, and salary pressures partially offset by a $2.2 million decrease in Social Assistance as clients transition to the AccessAbility Support Program.
  • Public Schools Branch and La Commission scolaire de langue française are forecasting a combined $3.0 million increase due to high diesel and heating fuel prices driven by global supply chain disruptions.
  • The Department of Justice and Public Safety is forecasting an expenditure increase of $2.1 million, primarily driven by $1.0 million in salary pressures due to lower vacancies than budgeted, $647 thousand in professional services, and $242 thousand for supplies due to higher correctional inmate bed days.
  • The Department of Transportation and Infrastructure is forecasting a net decrease in expenditures of $29.0 million. The reduction is primarily because major infrastructure projects are progressing more slowly than planned, delaying associated expenditures. These savings are partially offset by increased highway, bridge, line material, sand, and salary costs.
  • Interest charges on debt are forecasted to be $3.8 million over budget as borrowing rates for both debentures and short-term treasury notes are higher than assumed during budget preparation.

item.title: New coordinator role enhances support for medical first responders in PEI
item.description:
New coordinator role enhances support for medical first responders in PEI jenniferdhogan Fri, 10/30/2026 - 13:10

Kenneth Ramsay knows firsthand what it’s like to be the first person to arrive at an emergency scene.

Ramsay has helped Islanders through some of the most difficult moments of their lives. Whether stopping a severe bleed or providing lifesaving breaths, he has spent 21 years as a paramedic and 27 years as a volunteer firefighter serving his community. 

Now, Ramsay is bringing that experience to his new role as coordinator of the Medical First Responder (MFR) Program, a partnership between Island EMS, PEI Firefighters Association and the provincial government. The program ensures firefighters have the training they need to provide emergency medical care to people before paramedics reach the scene. 

“I have a personal interest in the program,” Ramsay said. “Over the years, while teaching firefighters to become medical first responders, I saw a lot of opportunities for growth in the program. I felt this was something I could make a difference in because I understand the program.”

Since starting this position in the spring, Ramsay has focused on building a strong foundation for the program. He is working with partners to establish an advisory committee, developing a new website, and supporting fire departments with day-to-day needs such as program resources and medical supplies, including AED pads, oxygen and trauma dressings. 

His goal is to create greater consistency across the province and ensure fire departments are aligned with Island EMS clinical practice guidelines.

“Right now, fire departments each have their own approaches and processes,” Ramsay said. “I would like to see it standardized, bring everyone on the same page, and make the whole emergency health system work better.”

PEI currently has 35 fire departments and hundreds of trained medical first responders who play a vital role in emergency response, particularly in rural communities where they are often among the first to arrive and begin patient care.

“Often, they’re on scene before the ambulance arrives and providing lifesaving care,” Ramsay said. “I’ve witnessed many instances where medical first responders have brought people back to life from cardiac arrest before paramedics arrived.”

When asked what message he would like Islanders to know about firefighters who serve as medical first responders, Ramsay’s answer is simple. 

“I want Islanders to know we will always be there for you. We will provide care to the best of our ability, and we will do so with compassion.”

Next steps include establishing the advisory committee and holding its first meeting before the end of the year to help guide the future direction of the program.   

“The goal is to create a more integrated medical first responder program that strengthens coordination between MFRs and Island EMS,” Ramsay said.

The coordinator position is funded by the provincial government as part of its investments to strengthen the MFR Program.

item.title: New resources available for farm succession planning on Prince Edward Island
item.description:
New resources available for farm succession planning on Prince Edward Island ddgillis Fri, 10/30/2026 - 11:15

Farmers preparing for ownership transition can access new resources to help them plan for passing on their farm business. 

The Step Toward the Future hub brings information and resources together in one place to help farmers think ahead, seek advice, and work through the decisions involved in succession. Producers can visit the hub to find upcoming workshops, access a free online succession-preparation course, and explore new planning tools and resources as they are added.

“Succession planning is vital for the continued sustainability and economic growth of our farming industry on Prince Edward Island,” said the Honourable Heath MacDonald, Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food. “With many producers retiring in the years ahead, this new hub will provide the information and resources to help new and aspiring farmers step into the industry with confidence and success.”

“Supporting the next generation of farmers continues to be a priority for Prince Edward Island. A strong future for Island agriculture depends on great planning today, and this succession planning hub will be a valuable resource as people prepare for the future of their farms.”

- Agriculture Minister Hilton MacLennan.

Succession isn’t just the transfer of tasks, skills, or assets; it is also the transfer of leadership. Succession planning ensures a smooth transition from an outgoing farmer or older generation to the next generation. More than 40 per cent of Canadian farm operators will retire in the next decade. On Prince Edward Island, only 10.5 per cent of farmers have a written succession plan, according to the 2021 census. The Step Toward the Future hub provides farmers with a clear path forward to support generational farming on Prince Edward Island. 

There will also be a series of information sessions this fall and next year to help guide farmers in their planning. 

The first Next Generation Farm Succession Workshop will take place on November 28 and will feature Patti Durand, a certified Family Enterprise Advisor who has guided hundreds of Canadian farm business families through transition planning and decision making.

“In 2024, PEI’s agriculture and agri-food exports reached $1.05 billion, the highest in the province’s history,” said Minister MacLennan. “With thoughtful succession planning, that growth can continue, farmers can stay confident, and the next generation can be set up for success.”

Producers are encouraged to check the Step Toward the Future hub regularly for updates on workshops, a succession planning guidebook, supplementary tools, and other resources.

The Step Toward the Future hub is funded in part by the Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership, 5-year, $3.5-billion investment by federal, provincial and territorial governments to strengthen competitiveness, innovation, and resiliency of Canada’s agriculture, agri‐food, and agri‐based products sector. This includes $1 billion in federal programs and activities and a $2.5-billion commitment that is cost-shared 60 per cent federally and 40 per cent provincially/territorially for programs that are designed and delivered by provinces and territories.

item.title: Premier McLeod on the Enbridge Line 21 Pipeline
item.description:
YELLOWKNIFE - Premier Bob McLeod issued the following statement on the Enbridge Line 21 pipeline today:

“I was pleased to learn that operations have resumed for Enbridge’s Line 21 pipeline after almost 2 years of no activity.

"Resource development has, and will continue to be, the backbone of our economy and is central to ensuring a good source of middle class jobs and business opportunities. Our territory has mineral and petroleum resources and the development of those resources can have a transformative effect on our people and economy.

"Sustainable economic development is key to the future of Northerners. With a strong resource development base, we will be able to support diversification of our local economies into emerging and established sectors.

"On behalf of the Government of the Northwest Territories I’d like to offer my congratulations to Imperial Oil, Enbridge the town of Norman Wells and other partners for getting this pipeline back up and running. I know the efforts and economic impacts of the pipeline have already begun to take shape in the community and will be felt for years to come. ”

 

Charlotte Digness
Media and Communications Coordinator
